title: Heartbleed: the bug that leaked the internet's memory

scenes.narration: [serious] One tiny mistake left the internet's locks leaking for two years.
Many websites use the same free code to keep your data safe. On New Year's Eve 2011, a programmer made a small mistake.
Nobody saw it. Then, in April 2014, experts at Google and another company found it. They called it Heartbleed.
The problem? Websites could be tricked into leaking secrets. About 17 out of 100 safe websites were open.
Canada's tax office lost data on about 900 people. It closed its website.
Police caught a 19-year-old from Ontario, Canada.
Half a million websites, all open because of one small mistake.

facts.claim: The Heartbleed code was committed on New Year's Eve 2011 and disclosed on April 7, 2014; fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.1g
About 17% (around half a million) of trusted SSL websites were vulnerable; up to 64 KB of memory could leak, including private keys
Programmer Robin Seggelmann wrote the code by mistake ('I missed validating a variable containing a length'); a reviewer also missed it; Google and Codenomicon researchers found it independently
The Canada Revenue Agency said about 900 people's social insurance numbers were stolen over six hours; it had shut down online services
The RCMP charged Stephen Solis-Reyes, 19, of London, Ontario, with unauthorized use of a computer and mischief in relation to data
